newsitem.title: INDIA: India's political crisis at impasse.
newsitem.headline: India's political crisis at impasse.

text.p: India's ruling United Front coalition and its rival, the Congress party, remained at loggerheads on Sunday ahead of a parliamentary confidence vote this week that will determine whether the 15-party government stands or falls.
"There is no breakthrough yet. It's a stalemate," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said.
"Mid-level talks not going anywhere. At the moment the stalemate is continuing if not deepening," a senior member of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition said.

The lower house of parliament has set Friday as the date for the vote on the 10-month-old government, which President Shankar Dayal Sharma called after Congress president Sitaram Kesri, citing economic drift and a vengeful United Front, announced his party was withdrawing its vital support for Deve Gowda.
The prime minister, whose coalition includes regional, communist and centrist parties, has depended on Congress's 140 votes in the 542-member assembly to survive.
The United Front controls 180 seats while the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is the biggest single party, controlling 193, including allies.
Congress has demanded that Deve Gowda quit, but the United Front has stood firm behind the prime minister, who was a surprise choice last June after an inconclusive general election.
The stalemate has made a hostage of an investor-friendly draft budget that would slash corporate and personal taxes.

Leaders of the rival camps have been meeting to try to achieve a power-sharing deal that would avert an early general election which public opinion polls indicate would boost the Hindu nationalist BJP's chances of returning to power.
But Kesri launched a broadside at Deve Gowda on Saturday, calling him inefficient and "communal" -- a reference to his alleged ties to the BJP.
All India Radio said the BJP's national executive decided on Sunday to "pull down the United Front government".
But the state radio station quoted a BJP spokeswoman as saying the party would stake a claim to power only if it was in a position to form a stable government.
The BJP ruled for 12 days last May but quit when it was unable to secure enough votes in the hung parliament to win a vote of confidence.
The United Front has repeatedly raised the threat of an early election in hopes of putting pressure on Congress, which would be expected to suffer the most if fresh polls were held now.
But Gadgil, who met Sharma on Saturday, said the president seemed keen to avoid such a step.
"As I was leaving, he told me it is not in the interest of the country to have mid-term elections," Gadgil told Reuters.
The United Front leader, who asked not to be named, said he saw no resolution of the impasse until shortly before the test vote.
"A formal understanding could be reached only on the 10th or 11th," he said. "The negotiating positions are so hard, they will hold out until the last."
